This page goes with **Chapter 14, Accompanimental Textures** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AccompanimentalTexture.html). Read each section there
first. The book shows each texture in notation and in recordings. Here you can **play** each one: the site's backing band plays the
same chords in each texture, and you switch between textures while it plays.

**How the demos work:** press **▶ Play**, then try the buttons under it. The band keeps going and changes texture at the next bar.
**Who plays** turns each part on and off. Under the buttons the last four bars the band played are written out, so you can see what
you hear. Tempo and Stop are in the strip at the bottom of the page. The [quiz](#quiz) at the end plays a texture without naming it, and
you say which one it is.

## 14.1 Texture

The book looks at texture two ways. **Vertically**: how many notes sound at once (how full the chords are, how many voices there are).
**Horizontally**: how busy the rhythm is (are the most common note values long or short?).
[Read 14.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Texture.html)

Below are the same four chords played three ways. Held chords are full but slow. Repeated eighth notes keep the same notes and make
the rhythm busy. An arpeggio is busy too, but it plays one note at a time, so it is thinner at any one moment.

## 14.2 Chorale texture

In a **chorale texture** there is a new chord for (nearly) every melody note, so all the parts move in the same rhythm. This is also
called **homorhythmic**. A hymn played on the piano is the plainest case. The band's hymn style below holds each chord until the next one,
with three voices over the bass. With a melody on top, it would be a chorale texture.
[Read 14.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ChoraleTexture.html) ·
[Pattern lesson: Hymn, four parts](../lessons/patterns/chords-hymn.qmd)

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="hymn" data-chart="C F|C G|Am Dm|G C" data-tempo="72" data-on="bass comp" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Played on:" data-choices='[{"label":"Piano","opts":{"calm":false}},{"label":"Quarter-note chords","opts":{"compRhythm":"quarters","calm":false}}]'></div>

The second button is the book's **quarter-note texture**: a chord on every beat. The book's practice exercises ask for it
(17.7, exercise 3).

## 14.3 Arpeggiated accompaniments

An **arpeggio** plays a chord's notes one after another instead of all together. The bass usually holds the root underneath, as in the
book's first example, Beethoven's *Moonlight Sonata*. The band can arpeggiate up and back down, or rock between the lowest and highest
notes. **Alberti bass** goes low, high, middle, high, again and again.
[Read 14.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ArpeggiatedAccompaniments.html) ·
Pattern lessons: [Arpeggio, up and down](../lessons/patterns/chords-arp.qmd) ·
[Arpeggio, low and high](../lessons/patterns/chords-arp2.qmd) ·
[Alberti bass](../lessons/patterns/chords-alberti.qmd)

## 14.4 Block chord accompaniments

**Block chords** strike all the notes of the chord together. What makes one block-chord accompaniment different from another is its
**rhythm**. The book names four:

- **"1 (2) &"**: two chords a bar, on beat 1 and on the and of 2. Count it aloud and stay silent on the number in brackets.
- **The "Barbara Ann" rhythm**, over two bars: **1 2 3 (4) & | (1) & (2) & 3**.
- **Repeated eighth-note chords**: a chord on every eighth note, in classical music and in rock.
- **Repeated quarter-note chords**: a chord on every beat.

[Read 14.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BlockChordAccompaniments.html) ·
Pattern lessons: [Charleston (the 1 (2) & rhythm)](../lessons/patterns/chords-charleston.qmd) ·
[Barbara Ann](../lessons/patterns/chords-barbara.qmd) ·
[Driving eighths](../lessons/patterns/chords-eighths.qmd) ·
[Quarter-note chords](../lessons/patterns/chords-quarters.qmd)

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="motown" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="100" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Rhythm:" data-choices='[{"label":"1 (2) &","opts":{"compRhythm":"charleston","bassFeel":"dotted","calm":false}},{"label":"Barbara Ann","opts":{"compRhythm":"barbara","bassFeel":"motown","calm":false}},{"label":"Repeated eighths","opts":{"compRhythm":"eighths","bassFeel":"eighths","calm":false}},{"label":"Repeated quarters","opts":{"compRhythm":"quarters","bassFeel":"roots","calm":false}}]'></div>

The band calls the "1 (2) &" rhythm the **Charleston**: jazz musicians use that name for the same two hits. The book points out that
the bass in "Let's Get It On" and "Thinking Out Loud" has a similar rhythm. The bass here plays the dotted 1, and of 2, 3 line with it.
Turn the drums and bass off to hear the chords alone.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## 14.5 Afterbeats and off-beats

**Afterbeats** is Arnold Schoenberg's word for repeated chords that come *after* the downbeat. **Off-beats** are chords that keep to
the upbeats and stay off the downbeats. The book looks at two styles built on off-beats: **polka** and **reggae**.
[Read 14.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AfterbeatsOffbeats.html) ·
Pattern lessons: [Boom-chick](../lessons/patterns/chords-oompah.qmd) ·
[Every off-beat](../lessons/patterns/chords-upbeats.qmd)

Polka: the bass on the beat and the chord in between. The band counts the bar in four, so the chords fall on 2 and 4. Counted in a fast
two, those are the off-beats.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="folk" data-chart="C|G7|G7|C" data-tempo="120" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choices='[{"label":"Bass and chords take turns","opts":{"bassFeel":"alt","compRhythm":"oompah"}},{"label":"Bass on every beat","opts":{"bassFeel":"polka","compRhythm":"oompah"}}]'></div>

Reggae: short chords on the and of every beat, often on electric guitar, over a drum part (the one-drop) that leaves beat 1 empty.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="reggae" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="76" data-comp="guitar" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp drums"></div>

## 14.6 The 3–2 son clave and 3+3+2

The **3–2 son clave** is a two-bar rhythm at the root of Afro-Cuban music: three strokes in the first bar and two in the second. Its
first bar divides eight eighth notes into **3+3+2**. In popular music it is also called the **Bo Diddley beat**. The 3+3+2 bar on its own
is everywhere in pop. In sixteenth notes it is called **tresillo**, and the book follows it into the habanera and the reggaeton beat.
[Read 14.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ThreeTwoClave.html) ·
Pattern lessons: [3–2 clave in the chords](../lessons/patterns/chords-clave32.qmd) ·
[3+3+2](../lessons/patterns/chords-tresillo.qmd) ·
[The Bo Diddley beat on drums](../lessons/patterns/drums-bodiddley.qmd) ·
[Dembow (reggaeton)](../lessons/patterns/drums-dembow.qmd)

The book's section has more than thirty examples. The full list, with notation of each rhythm, is in
[14.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ThreeTwoClave.html).
:::

## 14.7 Distinctive bass lines

Some songs are known by their **riff**: a short bass (or guitar) figure repeated under the chords. The band's bass lines are not those
riffs. They are general patterns that fit any chords. But they show how much of a style's character comes from a repeating bass figure.
Drums and bass only:
[Read 14.7](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DistinctiveBassLines.html)

## Quiz: name the texture {#quiz}

Press **New texture**. The band plays a progression in one of the textures below without naming it, and you pick which one. Listen for
two things: are the notes sounding together or one at a time, and where in the bar do the chords fall? The notes appear after you answer.
**▶ Again** replays the same one.

Piano textures (14.2, 14.3, 14.4):

<div class="ar-quiz" data-style="hymn" data-tempo="84" data-on="bass comp" data-staves="comp bass" data-charts="C|Am|F|G;C|F|G|C;Am|Dm|E|Am;F|Dm|Bb|C;G|Em|C|D" data-choices='[{"label":"Chorale (held chords)","why":"One chord struck and held for each harmony.","opts":{"compRhythm":"hymn","calm":false}},{"label":"Quarter-note chords","why":"The whole chord on every beat.","opts":{"compRhythm":"quarters","calm":false}},{"label":"Repeated eighths","why":"The whole chord on every eighth note.","opts":{"compRhythm":"eighths","calm":false}},{"label":"Arpeggio","why":"One note at a time, up the chord and back down.","opts":{"compRhythm":"arp","calm":false}},{"label":"Alberti bass","why":"One note at a time: low, high, middle, high.","opts":{"compRhythm":"alberti","calm":false}}]'></div>

Rhythms (14.4, 14.5, 14.6). The chords play the rhythm over held bass notes, with no drums, so the rhythm is all in the chords:

<div class="ar-quiz" data-style="hymn" data-tempo="96" data-on="bass comp" data-staves="comp" data-charts="C|Am|F|G;C|F|G|C;Am|Dm|E|Am;F|Dm|Bb|C;G|Em|C|D" data-choices='[{"label":"1 (2) &","why":"Beat 1 and the and of 2.","opts":{"compRhythm":"charleston","calm":false}},{"label":"Barbara Ann","why":"1 2 3 (4) & | (1) & (2) & 3.","opts":{"compRhythm":"barbara","calm":false}},{"label":"Off-beats","why":"The and of every beat, never on a beat.","opts":{"compRhythm":"upbeats","calm":false}},{"label":"Boom-chick (2 and 4)","why":"Chords on 2 and 4, between the bass notes.","opts":{"compRhythm":"oompah","calm":false}},{"label":"3+3+2","why":"Beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4: eight eighths grouped 3+3+2.","opts":{"compRhythm":"tresillo","calm":false}},{"label":"3–2 son clave","why":"1, the and of 2, 4 | 2, 3.","opts":{"compRhythm":"clave32","calm":false}}]'></div>

## For teachers

- **The band:** the demos run on the site's [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd) band. Each button changes one band setting
  (comping rhythm, bass line or drum groove) and the change takes effect at the next bar. The same patterns, each with a step-by-step
  lesson, are on the [Pattern lessons](../lessons/patterns/index.qmd) pages.
- **Names:** the band's names for some rhythms differ from the book's. The book's "1 (2) &" is the band's *Charleston*, its afterbeats in
  polka are the band's *boom-chick*, and its reggae off-beats are the band's *every off-beat*. The quiz uses the book's names.
- **Not here:** the band does not play the book's specific songs or riffs (14.7), afterbeats as passing figures in thirds (the Mozart
  example in 14.5), or 3+3+2 in sixteenth notes against a slow beat. The book's listening lists are much longer than the selections here.
- **Videos:** the clips use the book's YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube. "Pretty Thing"
  (14.6) is no longer available there, so it is left out.
- **Not checked by ear:** the patterns were checked in notation and by the band's tests. Whether each one sounds like the book's examples
  has not been checked by listening.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
